intro: Martin Wörner plays Rachmaninoff’s Prelude in C♯ minor, Op. 3 No. 2, in a private recording made in May 2005. The piece opens with three notes, moves into a rush of triplets and ends with a return in very large chords.

sections.label: A · Bells, then rushing triplets
sections.mNote: A–G♯–C♯ leads into the quiet chordal reply.

sections.label: B · Agitato, triplet figuration
sections.mNote: The central Agitato rises in triplets to descending chords.

sections.label: C · Return of the bell chords
sections.mNote: The opening chords return, written across four staves.

sections.label: D · Quiet chords over C♯
sections.mNote: A low C♯ holds beneath the final chords.

cues.title: Opening three-note figure
cues.text: The figure A–G♯–C♯ falls in octaves, marked fortissimo. The chords that follow are marked ppp, and the three-note figure returns beneath them.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody in the central Agitato
cues.text: In the central Agitato, bars 14–34, the melody sits within running triplets. The tune is carried by long notes at the top of the right hand, stemmed separately above the triplets. The left hand plays phrases in reply, and the melody rises.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, Agitato, bars 14–34: upper melody separately stemmed above triplets, with left-hand answers. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening, bars 45–54
cues.text: At the Tempo primo, bars 45–54, the opening material returns written out on four staves, two for each hand. Rachmaninoff marks it fff pesante, very loud and heavy. The chords that were quiet on the first page now span the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, Tempo primo, bars 45–54: four-stave notation and fff pesante. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing chords over low C♯
cues.text: The last slow chords share a held low C♯. Above it, the hands move through a short succession of harmonies to the final C♯ minor chord. The dynamic returns to ppp.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: held low C♯, closing chords and final ppp. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
